aiGenerationNote: Create a 12-minute animated explainer video. Start with clear definitions of Reliability, HA, Fault Tolerance, and DR using simple analogies (e.g., a car with a spare tire for HA, a self-driving car for fault tolerance, moving to a new city after a disaster for DR). Visually represent RPO and RTO using a timeline and data loss/downtime indicators. Dedicate a segment to the AWS Well-Architected Framework's Reliability Pillar, showing its key principles as bullet points with brief visual cues. Conclude with a "Common Mistakes" section, highlighting the difference between HA and DR, and the importance of RPO/RTO. Include captions and a transcript.

screens.title: Reliability, High Availability & Disaster Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we will build a clear, practical understanding of three tightly related ideas that shape how you design and operate systems on AWS: reliability, high availability, and disaster recovery. Reliability is about a system doing its job consistently over time. High availability focuses on keeping the service accessible for a very large fraction of time, often expressed as "nines." Disaster recovery covers how you restore operations after a major regional or datacenter-level failure. We will also make two operational metrics central to your decisions: Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective, which define acceptable data loss and acceptable downtime. Throughout the module you will see concrete, business-driven examples and one realistic scenario to analyze. That scenario connects a stakeholder requirement to concrete design choices so you can practice translating RPO and RTO into replication, backup, and automation patterns. By the end you will be able to explain trade-offs between redundancy and cost, identify common mistakes teams make, and apply the Reliability Pillar principles to plan tests and automation. Think about a service you manage now and how these concepts would change its architecture. How much downtime and data loss would your business actually tolerate?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Business continuity depends on clear recovery targets and architecture choices that map to those targets. Reliability, HA, and DR are distinct but complementary.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Introduction
Reliability, High Availability & Disaster Recovery
Understand definitions, RPO/RTO metrics, and the Reliability Pillar guidance to design resilient AWS systems that meet business needs.
In this lesson
Translate recovery targets into architecture choices and validate them with tests.
Coming up
RPO and RTO examples, the Reliability Pillar, and a scenario analysis exercise.
Why it matters
Avoid over- or under-engineering and align costs to acceptable risk levels.
Reliability overview
Shared responsibility: AWS for the cloud, you for in-cloud configuration and operations.
High availability reduces downtime with redundancy and failover.
Fault tolerance aims to eliminate interruption for specific failure modes.
Disaster recovery restores operations after region-scale failures, guided by RPO and RTO.
Explore Key Topics
Definitions
Clear meanings for reliability, HA, fault tolerance and disaster recovery help you design appropriately.
RPO & RTO
Two business-driven metrics that determine backup frequency and recovery speed.
Reliability Pillar
Operational principles: automatic recovery, testing, horizontal scaling, and automation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define and distinguish reliability, high availability, fault tolerance, and disaster recovery in cloud environments. You will explain RPO and RTO, giving concrete examples of acceptable data loss and allowable downtime and describing how those numbers shape backup and replication strategy. You will understand the Reliability Pillar of the Well-Architected Framework and its practical principles such as automatic recovery, testing recovery procedures, horizontal scaling, and automation to manage change. Finally, you'll be able to identify common operational pitfalls that reduce availability, such as confusing HA with DR or failing to set RPO and RTO up front. Each objective pairs a conceptual definition with a practical outcome: you'll not only explain the terms but also map them to design choices and tests. This helps you avoid both costly overengineering and dangerous under-preparation. Expect to practice translating business requirements into architecture patterns and to reason about trade-offs between cost and resilience.

screens.title: Reliability: What it means in the cloud
screens.narratorSegment: Reliability is the system property that it will perform its intended function correctly and consistently over time. In operational terms this means fewer failures, predictable behavior under load, and repeatable outputs for the same inputs. Reliability is built from good design, defensive coding, predictable deployment automation, and monitoring. For example, a payment processing service that reliably accepts and confirms transactions during peak hours demonstrates reliability: customers experience the expected outcome without errors. One important nuance is the shared responsibility model: AWS provides reliable infrastructure, but you are responsible for reliability in your applications — choices like redundancy, health checks, deployments, and configuration management. A common misconception is treating reliability as a one-time project; in reality, it is an ongoing operational discipline. You measure reliability through metrics such as error rates, successful transaction counts, and service availability over time. To improve it, you reduce single points of failure, add retries and graceful degradation, and automate recovery actions so manual steps do not become the failure mode. Consider your monitoring alerts: are they focused on symptoms or on business impact? Reliable systems surface the impact to help teams prioritize fixes. Reflect on one recent outage and ask which design choices could have prevented it.

keyIdea.title: Definition in practice
keyIdea.text: Reliability is ongoing system correctness and consistency; it results from design, automation, monitoring, and operational discipline.

content.html:
Core Concept › Reliability
Reliability: consistent correct behavior
A reliable system minimizes failure frequency and impact through design and operational practices.
  • Measure reliability with error rates, successful transactions, and uptime trends.
  • Reduce single points of failure and automate repetitive tasks and recoveries.
  • Use monitoring that maps technical symptoms to business impact for effective prioritization.
Concrete example
A checkout service that validates and records orders reliably during a sale by using health checks, retries, and idempotent operations.
Key Takeaway

Reliability is a continuous practice: design, measure, automate, and improve.

Operational checklist
Design
Avoid single points of failure; favor horizontal scaling and stateless services.
Automation
Use automated deployments, health checks, and self-healing scripts to reduce manual intervention.
Monitoring
Track both technical metrics and business-level success metrics for a full view of reliability.
Misconception
Reliability is not just uptime; it includes correctness and consistent output under expected conditions.

screens.title: High Availability: "Nines" and redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: High availability focuses on keeping a service accessible and operational for a very large percentage of time. We measure availability in 'nines' — for example, 99.9% means a small permitted downtime over a defined period. HA is achieved by reducing the blast radius of component failures with redundancy and automatic failover. A common, practical approach on AWS is deploying across multiple Availability Zones so an instance, storage, or load balancer failure in one zone does not take down the whole service. HA designs accept that some components will fail and plan instant or near-instant replacement or redirection. A frequent misunderstanding is to equate HA with no outages; HA reduces but does not always eliminate downtime, especially for large-scale events. Designing for HA requires trade-offs: more redundancy increases cost and operational complexity. Measure availability continuously, and plan health checks and failover policies so that the system fails over safely. Ask stakeholders how much downtime they can tolerate, then select redundancy and failover designs that meet that percentage while keeping an eye on cost-effectiveness. High Availability: "Nines" and redundancy means high availability uses redundancy and failover to meet business uptime targets, often expressed as 'nines'.. In practical terms, what ha means and a practical view of availability targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: HA in practical terms
keyIdea.text: High availability uses redundancy and failover to meet business uptime targets, often expressed as 'nines'.

content.html:
Definition › High Availability
High Availability and 'nines'
Availability targets are business choices. Redundancy and quick failover help meet those targets.
Design for redundancy across components and zones to reduce single-point failures.
Use health checks and automated failover to restore service quickly.
Balance increased cost of redundancy against the business value of higher availability.
Concrete example
Deploying application instances in multiple Availability Zones so an AZ outage affects only a subset and traffic shifts without manual steps.
Common misconception
HA addresses component and AZ failures, not necessarily full regional disasters. For region-level outages you need a disaster recovery plan.
Check your understanding
If a single AZ fails, will your service remain reachable? If not, identify the single point of failure.

screens.title: Fault Tolerance: continuing operations during failures
screens.narratorSegment: Fault tolerance is the quality of a system to continue operating without interruption when one or more components fail. While high availability reduces downtime through rapid failover, fault tolerant systems are designed so that specific failures do not cause any interruption at all for covered failure modes. An example from storage is having mirrored disks so if one disk fails the other serves requests without a gap. The chapter mentions Amazon S3 as an inherently fault-tolerant service because it replicates data across multiple devices and facilities. Fault tolerance typically requires redundancy that can take over instantly. The trade-off is cost and complexity, since complete fault tolerance often duplicates components and paths. A common pitfall is assuming every part of a system needs full fault tolerance; in practice you target fault tolerance for the most critical, latency-sensitive pieces. Another misconception is thinking fault tolerance removes all operational risk; it mitigates certain failures but not human misconfiguration or catastrophic regional events. The right choice depends on business impact, cost, and acceptable residual risk. Fault Tolerance: continuing operations during failures means fault tolerance aims for uninterrupted operation for specific failure modes, often at higher cost and complexity than ha.. In practical terms, how it differs from ha and when it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fault tolerance explained
keyIdea.text: Fault tolerance aims for uninterrupted operation for specific failure modes, often at higher cost and complexity than HA.

content.html:
Definition › Fault Tolerance
Fault tolerance vs high availability
Fault tolerance seeks to avoid interruption entirely for certain failures; HA accepts small interruptions and recovers quickly.
  • Instant takeover via redundant components is the hallmark of fault tolerance.
  • It often requires duplication and careful orchestration to prevent split-brain or data inconsistency.
  • Apply it selectively to systems where any interruption is unacceptable.
Concrete example
Storage that mirrors data across devices so reads and writes continue immediately if one device fails, keeping user experience uninterrupted.
Precise note
Services such as Amazon S3 are designed to be fault-tolerant by replicating data across devices and facilities.
Misconception
Fault tolerance does not guarantee protection against every failure type, such as human configuration errors or regional disasters.

screens.title: Disaster Recovery: recovering from regional failures
screens.narratorSegment: Disaster recovery is the set of activities and design choices that restore operations after catastrophic events that affect an entire region or datacenter. The goal of DR is to resume business-critical functions at an alternate location, often a different AWS Region, within business-agreed recovery time and point targets. DR differs from HA in scope: HA handles component or AZ failures within a region, while DR prepares for large-scale outages that make the original location unusable. Effective DR planning starts with business-driven RPO and RTO targets. Those targets determine whether you need frequent backups, continuous replication, or a full warm standby in another region. A common trap is assuming that multi-AZ deployment is sufficient for DR; it is not. Another pitfall is having an untested plan — a DR document that has never been executed leaves you unprepared. DR also demands operational readiness: automation, clear runbooks, and proven procedures to restore services with confidence. Ultimately, DR balances cost, acceptable downtime, and acceptable data loss according to business priorities. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DR scope
keyIdea.text: Disaster recovery restores operations after large geographic failures and must be driven by RPO/RTO targets and validated through tests.

content.html:
Definition › Disaster Recovery
Disaster Recovery essentials
DR restores operations at an alternate location after a large-scale failure, guided by RPO and RTO.
  • Define RPO and RTO with stakeholders before designing DR.
  • Choose replication and backup strategies that meet those targets.
  • Automate recovery steps and test them regularly.
Concrete note
DR often involves restoring operations in another AWS Region; the exact approach depends on acceptable downtime and data loss.
Pitfalls
Confusing HA with DR or failing to test recovery procedures are common mistakes that make DR ineffective.
Action
Write a short runbook for restoring a critical service and schedule a dry run to validate it.

screens.title: RPO and RTO: defining recovery metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective are two simple but powerful business inputs to architecture. RPO defines the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time. If stakeholders set an RPO of five minutes, you must ensure backups or replication that limit data loss to no more than five minutes. RTO defines the maximum tolerable downtime. If the RTO is 4 hours, your recovery procedures, automation, and orchestration must be able to meet that window. These metrics are not technical defaults; they reflect business priorities and trade-offs. A lower RPO typically requires more frequent backups or continuous replication, increasing cost and complexity. A lower RTO requires faster automated recovery steps and perhaps standby capacity, also increasing cost. To choose RPO and RTO, start with impact analysis: what revenue, reputation, or legal risk does different downtime or data loss create? Translate those impacts into numbers your finance and product stakeholders approve. Then design the technical solution to meet those numbers and build tests that measure whether the recovery actions actually achieve the desired RPO and RTO. A common error is designing without these targets and ending up either overbuilt or insufficiently resilient.

keyIdea.title: RPO & RTO basics
keyIdea.text: RPO is acceptable data loss; RTO is acceptable downtime. Both must be defined by the business before designing a solution.

content.html:
Process Flow › RPO & RTO
Define RPO and RTO
Start with business impact, not technology. Convert impact tolerances into time windows for data loss and downtime.
  1. Identify business processes and acceptable loss/downtime.
  2. Translate those limits into RPO and RTO values with stakeholders.
  3. Design backups, replication, and automation to meet those values.
Operational consequences
Lower RPO: more frequent backups or continuous replication. Lower RTO: faster automation, standby capacity, and tested runbooks.
Concrete example
If an e-commerce sale demands at most 5 minutes of order loss, plan replication and backup frequency accordingly and test the failover path to ensure recovery within the allowed downtime.
Misconception
RPO and RTO are technical knobs; they are business-defined targets that drive technical design.

screens.title: Designing to meet RPO & RTO
screens.narratorSegment: Once RPO and RTO are defined, choose technical patterns that meet them. For RPO, think about how often data is persisted and whether replication is synchronous or asynchronous. A low RPO often means near-continuous replication or very frequent snapshots. For RTO, design the recovery path and automate it: scripted infrastructure deployment, automated DNS failover, and pre-provisioned capacity all shorten restoration time. Backups influence RPO directly: more frequent backups reduce potential data loss. Replication influences both RPO and service continuity: synchronous replication can reduce RPO to near zero but may add latency; asynchronous replication minimizes write latency but can allow some data loss. Automation is critical to meeting RTO: manual playbooks are slow and error-prone. Testing your recovery procedure is the final step. Run drills that simulate realistic failures and measure whether the RPO and RTO targets hold. A frequent operational mistake is designing without tests, which leaves uncertainty about whether the chosen patterns actually work under pressure. Use tests to tune frequency, replication mode, and automation until they reliably meet targets. Designing to meet RPO & RTO means backups set rpo limits; replication and automation determine whether you can meet rto and minimize data loss.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Map patterns to objectives
keyIdea.text: Backups set RPO limits; replication and automation determine whether you can meet RTO and minimize data loss.

content.html:
Process Flow › Meeting RPO & RTO
Choose replication and backup modes
Synchronous replication reduces data loss but can add latency. Asynchronous replication lowers latency but increases RPO risk.
Frequent backups lower RPO but may increase storage and processing costs.
Replication across locations reduces risk of single-site loss but can complicate consistency guarantees.
Automate recovery to meet RTO
Pre-script deployments, automate DNS and routing changes, and maintain tested runbooks. Manual steps slow recovery and increase error risk.
Testing
Run realistic recovery drills to measure whether your design actually meets RPO and RTO. Adjust backup frequency and automation until tests pass.
Pro tip
Target fault tolerance only for components where uninterrupted service justifies the extra cost.

screens.title: Reliability Pillar: operational principles
screens.narratorSegment: The Reliability Pillar of the Well-Architected Framework gives practical principles to guide resilient designs. Key principles include automatically recovering from failure, testing recovery procedures regularly, scaling horizontally to increase aggregate availability, avoiding guessing capacity, and managing change through automation. Automatic recovery reduces mean time to repair by letting systems self-heal rather than requiring operator intervention. Testing recovery exercises the runbooks and validates assumptions such as how long restoration actually takes. Horizontal scaling distributes load, so single component failures have less impact on overall capacity. Avoiding guessed capacity means measure actual usage and scale in response to demand rather than provisioning too much or too little. Finally, managing change with automated deployments and validated pipelines prevents human error from becoming the weakest link in availability. These principles are operational: they affect monitoring design, deployment pipelines, and runbook practice. Apply them iteratively: adopt automation for the riskiest manual processes first, then expand testing and scaling practices as you gain confidence. screens.title: Common pitfalls: HA vs DR and testing gaps
screens.narratorSegment: Teams commonly make three recurring mistakes when planning for resilience. First, confusing high availability with disaster recovery. HA reduces downtime for component and AZ failures, but it does not protect against an entire region going offline; DR requires recovery at another location. Second, failing to define RPO and RTO before designing solutions. Without those targets, teams either over-engineer resilience at unnecessary cost or under-engineer and leave the business exposed. Third, not testing recovery procedures. A documented DR plan that has never been exercised offers no assurance that recovery steps will work under pressure. Avoid these pitfalls by always starting from business requirements, documenting explicit RPO and RTO values, and scheduling regular recovery drills. Use automation to make recovery repeatable and reduce human error. When testing, measure actual recovery time and data loss against the stated objectives and iterate on the architecture and playbooks until they meet the targets reliably. This disciplined approach turns resilience from a vague goal into verifiable outcomes. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we will build a clear, practical understanding of three tightly related ideas that shape how you design and operate systems on AWS: reliability, high availability, and disaster recovery. Reliability is about a system doing its job consistently over time. High availability focuses on keeping the service accessible for a very large fraction of time, often expressed as "nines." Disaster recovery covers how you restore operations after a major regional or datacenter-level failure. We will also make two operational metrics central to your decisions: Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective, which define acceptable data loss and acceptable downtime. Throughout the module you will see concrete, business-driven examples and one realistic scenario to analyze. That scenario connects a stakeholder requirement to concrete design choices so you can practice translating RPO and RTO into replication, backup, and automation patterns. By the end you will be able to explain trade-offs between redundancy and cost, identify common mistakes teams make, and apply the Reliability Pillar principles to plan tests and automation. Think about a service you manage now and how these concepts would change its architecture. How much downtime and data loss would your business actually tolerate?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define and distinguish reliability, high availability, fault tolerance, and disaster recovery in cloud environments. You will explain RPO and RTO, giving concrete examples of acceptable data loss and allowable downtime and describing how those numbers shape backup and replication strategy. You will understand the Reliability Pillar of the Well-Architected Framework and its practical principles such as automatic recovery, testing recovery procedures, horizontal scaling, and automation to manage change. Finally, you'll be able to identify common operational pitfalls that reduce availability, such as confusing HA with DR or failing to set RPO and RTO up front. Each objective pairs a conceptual definition with a practical outcome: you'll not only explain the terms but also map them to design choices and tests. This helps you avoid both costly overengineering and dangerous under-preparation. Expect to practice translating business requirements into architecture patterns and to reason about trade-offs between cost and resilience.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and validation. You will analyze a scenario that gives explicit recovery constraints and then map those constraints to concrete architecture choices and monitoring practices. That exercise asks you to identify the RPO and RTO, then list at least three services or patterns you would use and justify how each contributes to meeting those targets. Practicing this translation trains you to start every design from business goals rather than technical assumptions. You will also review common assessment items that check whether you correctly identify RPO and RTO from stakeholder statements and whether you understand which strategies protect against AZ-level failures versus region-level disasters. Finally, you will learn to write and schedule recovery tests. Testing is essential because a documented plan that is never executed provides no assurance. These practice outcomes keep the focus on repeatable, verifiable competency rather than vague claims about resilience.

Reliability is the system property that it will perform its intended function correctly and consistently over time. In operational terms this means fewer failures, predictable behavior under load, and repeatable outputs for the same inputs. Reliability is built from good design, defensive coding, predictable deployment automation, and monitoring. For example, a payment processing service that reliably accepts and confirms transactions during peak hours demonstrates reliability: customers experience the expected outcome without errors. One important nuance is the shared responsibility model: AWS provides reliable infrastructure, but you are responsible for reliability in your applications — choices like redundancy, health checks, deployments, and configuration management. A common misconception is treating reliability as a one-time project; in reality, it is an ongoing operational discipline. You measure reliability through metrics such as error rates, successful transaction counts, and service availability over time. To improve it, you reduce single points of failure, add retries and graceful degradation, and automate recovery actions so manual steps do not become the failure mode. Consider your monitoring alerts: are they focused on symptoms or on business impact? Reliable systems surface the impact to help teams prioritize fixes. Reflect on one recent outage and ask which design choices could have prevented it.

High availability focuses on keeping a service accessible and operational for a very large percentage of time. We measure availability in 'nines' — for example, 99.9% means a small permitted downtime over a defined period. HA is achieved by reducing the blast radius of component failures with redundancy and automatic failover. A common, practical approach on AWS is deploying across multiple Availability Zones so an instance, storage, or load balancer failure in one zone does not take down the whole service. HA designs accept that some components will fail and plan instant or near-instant replacement or redirection. A frequent misunderstanding is to equate HA with no outages; HA reduces but does not always eliminate downtime, especially for large-scale events. Designing for HA requires trade-offs: more redundancy increases cost and operational complexity. Measure availability continuously, and plan health checks and failover policies so that the system fails over safely. Ask stakeholders how much downtime they can tolerate, then select redundancy and failover designs that meet that percentage while keeping an eye on cost-effectiveness. High Availability: "Nines" and redundancy means high availability uses redundancy and failover to meet business uptime targets, often expressed as 'nines'.. In practical terms, what ha means and a practical view of availability targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fault tolerance is the quality of a system to continue operating without interruption when one or more components fail. While high availability reduces downtime through rapid failover, fault tolerant systems are designed so that specific failures do not cause any interruption at all for covered failure modes. An example from storage is having mirrored disks so if one disk fails the other serves requests without a gap. The chapter mentions Amazon S3 as an inherently fault-tolerant service because it replicates data across multiple devices and facilities. Fault tolerance typically requires redundancy that can take over instantly. The trade-off is cost and complexity, since complete fault tolerance often duplicates components and paths. A common pitfall is assuming every part of a system needs full fault tolerance; in practice you target fault tolerance for the most critical, latency-sensitive pieces. Another misconception is thinking fault tolerance removes all operational risk; it mitigates certain failures but not human misconfiguration or catastrophic regional events. The right choice depends on business impact, cost, and acceptable residual risk. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Disaster recovery is the set of activities and design choices that restore operations after catastrophic events that affect an entire region or datacenter. The goal of DR is to resume business-critical functions at an alternate location, often a different AWS Region, within business-agreed recovery time and point targets. DR differs from HA in scope: HA handles component or AZ failures within a region, while DR prepares for large-scale outages that make the original location unusable. Effective DR planning starts with business-driven RPO and RTO targets. Those targets determine whether you need frequent backups, continuous replication, or a full warm standby in another region. A common trap is assuming that multi-AZ deployment is sufficient for DR; it is not. Another pitfall is having an untested plan — a DR document that has never been executed leaves you unprepared. DR also demands operational readiness: automation, clear runbooks, and proven procedures to restore services with confidence. Ultimately, DR balances cost, acceptable downtime, and acceptable data loss according to business priorities. Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective are two simple but powerful business inputs to architecture. RPO defines the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time. If stakeholders set an RPO of five minutes, you must ensure backups or replication that limit data loss to no more than five minutes. RTO defines the maximum tolerable downtime. If the RTO is 4 hours, your recovery procedures, automation, and orchestration must be able to meet that window. These metrics are not technical defaults; they reflect business priorities and trade-offs. A lower RPO typically requires more frequent backups or continuous replication, increasing cost and complexity. A lower RTO requires faster automated recovery steps and perhaps standby capacity, also increasing cost. To choose RPO and RTO, start with impact analysis: what revenue, reputation, or legal risk does different downtime or data loss create? Translate those impacts into numbers your finance and product stakeholders approve. Then design the technical solution to meet those numbers and build tests that measure whether the recovery actions actually achieve the desired RPO and RTO. A common error is designing without these targets and ending up either overbuilt or insufficiently resilient.

Once RPO and RTO are defined, choose technical patterns that meet them. For RPO, think about how often data is persisted and whether replication is synchronous or asynchronous.
